title: Falmouth at the Licking Forks
summary: Falmouth was established in 1793 at the confluence of the Main Licking and South Licking in what became Pendleton County. Virginians who settled there named it for Falmouth in…
bodyMarkdown:
Falmouth sits where two rivers become one. The Main Licking and the South Licking meet here in Pendleton County, and the town has stood at that meeting since 1793. Virginians who settled the spot named it for Falmouth in Stafford County, back home.

Long before there was a town, the forks were a landing. In June 1780 the British commander at Detroit sent [Capt. Henry Bird](/people/#henry-bird) south by water with Canadian rangers, cannon, and a large force of Native allies. The [state marker on Main Street](https://history.ky.gov/markers/birds-war-road-june-1780) names Shawnee, Ottawa, Huron, Chippewa, Delaware, and Mingo warriors among them.

Bird's force landed near the forks and marched south toward the Kentucky stations. At [Ruddell's Station](/stories/isaac-ruddell-and-the-guns-at-ruddells-station/) and Martin's Station, artillery broke log walls that had never faced guns. The raiders came back to the forks with hundreds of captives. A [second marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/british-indian-raid) says the captives were divided there and families separated.

Some went to Detroit, and others were scattered among Native towns north of the Ohio.

The markers do not agree on the numbers. One counts 200 rangers and 600 warriors with 400 captives. The other counts 150 troops, 1,000 warriors, and 470 settlers taken. Both agree on what happened at the forks.

Peace brought a town. Among Falmouth's founders was John Waller, a Revolutionary veteran and legislator who [owned a gristmill and sawmill](https://secure.kentucky.gov/kyhs/hmdb/MarkerSearch.aspx?county=96&mode=County) on the South Fork of Licking. In 1798 Kentucky formed Pendleton County from parts of Bracken and Campbell. The county was organized in 1799 and named for [Edmund Pendleton](/people/#edmund-pendleton), the Virginia statesman who led the convention that ratified the federal Constitution. Falmouth has been the county seat ever since.

War came back in September 1862, when local home guards skirmished with Confederate cavalry near town during the invasion of Kentucky. Today Falmouth still sits where the two Licking branches meet, about thirty-nine miles south of Cincinnati. Downstream the river runs on toward [Newport at the Licking mouth](/stories/newport-at-the-licking-mouth/), and upstream lies [Cynthiana](/stories/cynthiana-cynthia-anna-on-the-licking/).

## Kentucky today

Downtown Falmouth has several state markers. Marker #34, "Bird's War Road; June 1780," stands at Shelby and Main Streets. Marker #937, "County Named, 1798," is on the courthouse lawn. Marker #953, "British, Indian Raid," and #686, "CSA at Falmouth," stand along US 27. Marker #1911 for John Waller is about three miles south of town.
